cards.text: Welcome in, friend! These are proverbs of Solomon, king of Israel, copied down by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah (Proverbs 1:1; 25:1). First up, the wicked flee when no one pursues, like the guy who hears his boss say “got a minute?” and starts packing up his desk.

cards.question: The wicked run when nobody's even chasing them. How does the proverb picture the righteous?

cards.text: Next, a whole land. A land in rebellion has many rulers, one after another, like a REVOLVING DOOR with a crown on it.

cards.question: True or false: the proverb says a land stays in order by having a whole crowd of rulers.

cards.text: Now a leader, and not a good one. He's destitute himself, and he oppresses the poor.

cards.question: That leader who oppresses the poor is pictured as a driving rain. Rain usually means a harvest, but what does this rain leave behind?

cards.text: Then the law steps in. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law resist them.

cards.question: Evil men don't understand justice. Who does the proverb say comprehends fully?

cards.text: Then two men side by side, one poor and one rich. The proverb picks the poor one, and friend, it is NOT because of his bank account.

cards.question: Better a poor man who walks with ___ than a rich man whose ways are perverse.

cards.text: Next, a son. A discerning son keeps the law.

cards.question: True or false: a son who keeps company with gluttons brings honor to his father.

cards.text: Then a man getting rich by charging interest and usury. Stacking it up. Counting it twice. Counting it AGAIN.

cards.question: True or false: wealth piled up by interest and usury ends up laid up for one who is kind to the poor.

cards.text: Now a serious one, friend. “Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, even his prayer is detestable.”

cards.question: Someone leads the upright along the path of evil. What does the proverb say happens to him?

answers.text: He falls into his own pit

cards.question: True or false: the proverb says a rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him.
When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, men ___ themselves.

cards.text: He who conceals his sins will not prosper. I once hid a burnt batch under parchment paper, and the smoke alarm confessed for me.

cards.question: Whoever confesses and renounces his sins will find ___.

cards.text: Okay, friend, round two. Blessed is the man who is always reverent.

cards.question: Blessed is the man who is always reverent, but he who ___ his heart falls into trouble.

cards.text: Remember that bold lion from the very first line? A lion shows up again, and this time it is NOT a compliment.

cards.question: Who does the proverb say is like a roaring lion or a charging bear?

answers.text: A wicked ruler over a helpless people
An army camped outside the city
A fool who won't stop talking

cards.question: True or false: the leader who lacks judgment is the one the proverb says will prolong his days.

cards.text: Then a heavy one. “A man burdened by bloodguilt will flee into the Pit; let no one support him.”

cards.question: He who walks with integrity will be kept ___, but whoever is perverse in his ways will suddenly ___.

cards.text: Now some honest work. The one who works his land will have plenty of food.

cards.question: The one who works his land has plenty. What does the one who chases fantasies get his fill of?

cards.text: A faithful man will abound with blessings, but one eager to be rich will not go unpunished. That's the guy replying to every “YOU WON!” text from a number he doesn't know.

cards.question: Showing partiality is not good. True or false: the proverb says a man will still do wrong for a piece of bread.
True or false: the stingy man rushing after wealth knows full well that poverty is waiting for him.

cards.text: Then two kinds of friends: the one who tells me there's dough in my mustache, and the one who says “looking SHARP, Papa” and lets me walk into the room like that.

cards.question: One man rebukes, another flatters with his tongue. Who does the proverb say later finds more favor?

cards.text: Then a hard line. Someone robs his father or mother, saying, “It is not wrong,” and the proverb calls him a companion to the man who destroys.

cards.question: A greedy man stirs up strife. Who does the proverb say will prosper?

answers.text: He who trusts in the LORD

cards.text: He who trusts in himself is a fool, but one who walks in wisdom will be safe. I told myself once, “I don't NEED a timer,” and friend, the oven still hasn't let me live it down.

cards.question: Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need. True or false: the one who hides his eyes from the poor will receive many curses.
When the wicked come to power, people hide themselves; but when the wicked perish, the righteous ___.

findings.problem: The card says the land in rebellion has many rulers "one after another." Proverbs 28:2 only says "has many rulers." It doesn't say whether they come in succession or rule at the same time. Adding "one after another" stretches the text. The "REVOLVING DOOR" joke then rests on that added reading, so it presents an interpretation as if it were the text.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The true or false card repeats Proverbs 28:11 almost word for word ("the proverb says a rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him"). The right answer is True. Nothing sets it up, and it asks nothing about the picture or the meaning. It reads like a test question ("According to verse 11..."), not a storyteller pausing mid-passage.

rule.text: Ask from inside the passage, the way a storyteller pauses to let the listener lean in. The question comes out of the moment Papa Dorin just set up.

findings.problem: The story card cites Proverbs 28:23 but tells none of the verse. It is only a joke about "two kinds of friends." It also frames the verse as being about friends. The text says "He who rebukes a man" and "one who flatters with his tongue," and neither is called a friend.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: Several story cards are bare restatements of the verse with almost none of Papa Dorin's voice. Examples are stop 1 card 5 ("Now a leader, and not a good one..."), stop 1 card 7 ("Then the law steps in." followed by the verse word for word), stop 1 card 11 ("Next, a son. A discerning son keeps the law."), stop 2 card 1 ("Okay, friend, round two. Blessed is the man who is always reverent.") and stop 2 card 8 ("Now some honest work..."). These read as stripped down, not as a funny, fatherly storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
